name: reef_v1
description: Coral reef monitoring: an updated figure (2019 vs 2023), a conflict about different periods, two sources sharing an author, an independent outlet restating a finding, and a follow-up question that needs passages the first question did not.
padding: Field teams logged water clarity, transect coverage and equipment calibration notes for every dive. Logistics, permits and boat schedules are documented in the appendix and are not discussed further here.

documents.title: survey-2019.txt
paragraphs: Reef Survey 2019. Ocean warming increases coral bleaching across the northern reef. Bleaching affected 30 percent of surveyed sites in 2019.
Herbivorous fish populations remained stable across the northern reef in 2019, with parrotfish grazing algae on damaged sections.
Nutrient runoff correlates with algae growth on damaged reef sections near river mouths during the wet season of 2019.

documents.title: survey-2023.txt
paragraphs: Reef Survey 2023. Ocean warming increases coral bleaching across the northern reef. Bleaching affected 61 percent of surveyed sites in 2023.
Marine heatwaves cause coral bleaching when temperatures stay above the seasonal maximum for several weeks in 2023.
Coral recovery depends on herbivorous fish populations that graze algae after bleaching events, according to the 2023 teams.

documents.title: review-2021.txt
paragraphs: Independent Reef Review 2021. Ocean warming does not increase coral bleaching at the southern sites, where cooler upwelling persisted from 2018 to 2020.
Fishing pressure reduces herbivorous fish populations near the harbour, which slows coral recovery after bleaching.

documents.title: news-2024.txt
paragraphs: Coastal News 2024. Ocean warming increases coral bleaching across the northern reef, scientists told reporters in 2024.

facts.text: Ocean warming increases coral bleaching across the northern reef.
Bleaching affected 30 percent of surveyed sites in 2019.
Bleaching affected 61 percent of surveyed sites in 2023.
Marine heatwaves cause coral bleaching when temperatures stay above the seasonal maximum for several weeks in 2023.
Ocean warming does not increase coral bleaching at the southern sites, where cooler upwelling persisted from 2018 to 2020.
Coral recovery depends on herbivorous fish populations that graze algae after bleaching events, according to the 2023 teams.
Fishing pressure reduces herbivorous fish populations near the harbour, which slows coral recovery after bleaching.
